title: “The Best Personal Statement of the Year”
subtitle: My personal statement for child psychiatry fellowship…
body_html:
The title of this piece was feedback on the personal statement that follows. It’s worth noting: I didn’t match at that program. But residents frequently ask me about the dreaded personal statement, and this is my second embarrassing installment. Here is what I wrote, way back when…in 2014. I do not love the writing in retrospect, but understand why I wrote it the way I did:

“Treatment delayed is treatment denied,” So said Rep. Tim Murphy from the floor of the House of Representatives, in a speech supporting his Helping Families in Mental Health Crisis Act. In that rare moment, the political process spoke directly to me and to why I am committed to training in child and adolescent psychiatry.

Comment: The someone else’s quote opener. Don’t do this. Please. It is a bad hook, and I provide your readers have read it a thousand times before.

Our current approach to mental illness has significant limitations, particularly with respect to delays in obtaining psychiatric care. My research work has focused on trying to better understand these delays in patients with first episode presentations of psychotic illnesses, which often occur in adolescents and transitional-age youth. We refer to this metric as Duration of Untreated Psychosis (DUP). Depending on the case, DUP can span weeks, months, or in many cases years. The reasons for this delay are complex. We do not fully understand the impact of DUP on outcomes in patients with psychotic illnesses, but emerging evidence suggests the longer the DUP, the worse the prognosis. As part of a team supervised by a pioneer in the field of pediatric schizophrenia, Dr. Christoph Correll, we are undertaking a comprehensive — hopefully definitive — meta-analysis of all the known studies in the literature on the subject of DUP. With over 600 individual papers on the subject, we certainly have our work cut out for us. However, the prospect of being able to shed some light on such a crucial topic for our field, and more importantly for our patients, is very rewarding. Given that many psychiatric illnesses first present in children and adolescents, I believe it is an area rich with possibilities for understanding — and then eliminating — barriers to obtaining effective treatment.

Comment: I did research. In the field in which I’m applying! Very impressive. I’m bored with myself already.

Once first-episode patients with psychiatric illnesses have been identified, I have learned that treating the current episode is never the whole story. It is in preventing relapse that we are able to offer real hope. I also believe that the most effective treatment options are often not, at first, the most palatable to the patient or their families. My research mentorship at Zucker Hillside Hospital with Drs. Correll and Kane has reinforced this. For patients with severe mental illness, preventing relapse is key to their long-term success. And yet I believe that in the U.S. we underutilize long-acting injectable (LAI) medications. Thus, I embarked on a study to ascertain what pediatric patients and their families would think about LAI formations of antipsychotic medications. The results were surprising: A significant proportion of patients, and over 30% of caregivers, believe LAI treatment offers benefits, yet we do not yet have research supporting their use in the population most likely to benefit from relapse prevention — those young patients with just one episode. Clearly, the path forward toward the best care for severely ill patients with mood and psychotic disorders isn't always easiest or most obvious treatment, and it will take well-informed child psychiatrists to advocate for these options.

Comment: Short, declarative sentences win over this argument any day. Split them in half? Adjectives abound!

First-episode patients have taught me the value of another core feature of child psychiatric practice: the family meeting. Without the support of families, it becomes highly unlikely that many patients will continue to follow our treatment plans. I have also found that the often-fraught environment of a difficult family meeting is an area in which I thrive, thanks in large part to my prior life as a improvisational performer in both jazz music and improv comedy.  Improvisational art forms taught me a simple lesson that has borne fruit in countless patient encounters: prepare beforehand, but in the moment it’s building on the ideas of others that counts. The other alternative, often practiced by doctors, is what fellow improv comedians refer to as “denial,” defined in this context as rejecting the perspective offered by others in favor of your own. Denial is improv comedy’s cardinal sin, and it reliably offers the most assured route to failure on the stage — and in the family meeting. One of my most memorable improv-informed family meetings involved a young woman with schizophrenia and her father who believed in “orthomolecular psychiatry.” Considering his worldview, I realized we might have common ground — how about the “natural” treatment with Omega-3 oils in addition to olanzapine? — which built enough of an alliance to bring her skeptical father into agreement with the team. In another case, in a family meeting with a first break mania patient's family in the ER, I recognized that, in this moment, they needed support as much as their admitted child did, and so I offered them the option of a Depression/Bipolar Support Alliance meeting for families happening that night that they could stop by on the way home. I also suggested they view a documentary about Bipolar Disorder called "Of Two Minds,” a movie I had also arranged for the Bipolar Clinic staff to view. 

Comment: I kinda can’t with this. I get it. I wrote a decent statement. But the self-promotion of these things is cringe-tastic.

Just as family meetings are a core of our clinical work, much of the rest of our practice takes place in the broader framework of schools, and interactions with schools are extremely important both for treatment and for advocacy. As a doctor who took the long road coming to medical school, I realize now that some of my pre-medicine experiences will prove helpful in my career as a child psychiatrist. I’ve already had significant experience interfacing with school systems. In my work in my early twenties at Litchfield Performing Arts, a non-profit dedicated to arts education, I found myself in the position of writing grants to fund projects we were pursuing to make the lives of school children better through the arts.  One notable project was funded in part through a WT Grant Foundation award I obtained called “Project Dance Live.” We worked with 12 academically and economically at-risk middle schoolers in the Waterbury, CT school systems, teaching academics (including didactics on essay writing I taught myself), dance, and workforce skills with the goal of high school retention and graduation. Over the course of this project and it’s parent project, Project Poetry Live, I worked with education researcher Dr. Martin Gardiner of Brown University to study our arts education program’s impact on the metrics of interest to decision makers — CT mastery test scores, as our main outcome variable. I found myself working closely with the administrators of seven Connecticut school districts to obtain the relevant data. I became well versed in the challenges faced by schools teaching troubled kids with limited resources. I also became familiar with how schools can effectively collaborate with researchers to support evidence-based projects that help kids grow in a resilient and enriched way. I also learned that building successful relationships with administrators and support staff is every bit as important to completing a project as writing the persuasive grant in the first place — without the buy-in of the teams at the schools, no research is possible.

A patient’s first experience with mental illness, which is often in childhood, is often terrifying. And it’s not just traumatic for the patient, but for their families. It also created difficulties in the larger structures of school, work, and relationships. Child Psychiatry training will provide me with the expertise to hone my pre-existing skills in humor, quick, “improvisational” thinking, systems-based care, and evidence-based practice in a way that can promote resiliency in the face of mental illness and demystify the road to recovery for patients and their caregivers.

Comment: I can stand behind this last paragraph to this day. For the rest…ugh. Personal statements are a brutal genre in hindsight.
